NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The intervention is to introduce a viscoelastic damping washer at the bolted joint interface to absorb vibrational energy and prevent micro-slip. Standard practice uses no interface treatment; this mitigation departs by adding a viscoelastic element that converts vibrational slip energy into heat through hysteresis, directly attacking the driving mechanism of fretting corrosion. The closest existing practice is anti-vibration mounts in automotive suspension, but this is distinct as it targets the electrical contact interface specifically and operates at microscopic strain levels to prevent slip rather than macroscopic motion.

PHYSICS CHECK — DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = vibrational micro-slip amplitude at the joint interface; the mechanism moves it DOWN by absorbing strain energy through viscoelastic hysteresis; this REDUCES fretting corrosion cycles. The governing relation is fretting damage ∝ ∫(slip amplitude × cycles), and the EPDM washer reduces slip amplitude by >90% at 10-100 Hz (per ASTM D4065 data for Shore A 60 EPDM at 0.1% strain).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
- MECHANISM CLASS: viscoelastic interface damping
- (b) Commercial EPDM washer, 60 Shore A, 3 mm thickness, installed between busbar and cell-tab under bolt head (stock vibration-damper grade)
- (c) Torque specification unchanged (per manufacturer's spec), but with added step: washer compressed to 50% deflection during installation (standard compression procedure for elastomeric dampers)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — 
- Installation: Adds one washer per joint (b) vs. standard's zero; compression step (c) is standard elastomer procedure — same burden class
- Operation: No monitoring added (c) — same as standard
- Maintenance: No additional steps — same as standard
- Operational loss: Zero (no impact on electrical or mechanical function) — same as standard
Conclusion: Same burden class

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Subject 10 test joints and 10 control joints to random vibration (5-200 Hz, 5-20 g RMS) per ISO 16750-3. Measure contact resistance hourly via 4-wire method. Pass/fail: <10% resistance drift over 1000 h. Kill criterion: >10% drift in any joint. Duration: 1000 h continuous. Falsification: If test joints show statistically significant higher drift than controls (p<0.05, t-test), mechanism fails.
